subject: Banking
title: Why Card Numbers Get Stolen
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Why Card Numbers Get Stolen.

hook.text: Your card number, expiry, and CVV are enough to buy anything online. Stolen card data sells for $5-20 on the dark web.

buildup.text: Data breaches at retailers expose millions of cards at once. The 2013 Target breach compromised 40 million cards.

discovery.text: Tokenization replaces your real number with a random token for each transaction. If stolen, the token is useless.

twist.text: Chip cards reduced in-store fraud 76%. But online fraud surged because criminals shifted to the easier target.

climax.text: Card security is a game of displacement. Fix one channel and fraud migrates to the next weakest link.

punchline.text: $5 for stolen card data. Fix stores, fraud moves online.

quiz.question: Why did online card fraud increase after chip cards were introduced?
options: Criminals shifted from harder in-store fraud to easier online fraud

details.summary: Card numbers are stolen through data breaches, skimming devices on ATMs, phishing attacks, and insecure online merchants. The fundamental vulnerability is that a static card number is enough to make purchases remotely.
details.whyItMatters: Card fraud costs the industry over 30 billion dollars annually. The root cause is that card numbers are shared secrets, once stolen, they can be reused until the card is cancelled, which is an outdated security model.
takeaways: A static 16-digit number plus expiry date is enough for online fraud
Skimmers on ATMs and gas pumps capture card data physically
Major data breaches have exposed hundreds of millions of card numbers

faq.question: Why haven't card companies fixed this problem?
faq.answer: Tokenization and EMV chips are partial fixes, but online transactions still rely on static numbers. Fully replacing the card number system would require rebuilding global payment infrastructure, which the industry has been slow to do.

faq.question: What should you do if your card number is stolen?
faq.answer: Contact your bank immediately to freeze the card. Review recent transactions for unauthorized charges. File disputes for any fraudulent transactions. Your liability is limited by law, but acting quickly minimizes hassle.
